Classic? I don’t get it! I hadn’t seen this old ‘classic’ film and was looking forward to watching it. However I was left feeling disappointed. As much as I watched ready to be impressed by the storyline or the acting performances, neither really stood the test of time for me. The story line was ok, but rather straightforward, and lacked the nuance or surprise I guess I’ve come to expect from a film like this. The acting felt just a little over exaggerated, each role neither felt a good reflection on the likely behaviour of people in that position, or had the depth of performance where the actor appears to have invested real emotional energy in the task. They were performances, more what I’d expect of the stage. Of course context is everything, and the context of watching this film back in the 50’s will likely of presented to me a very different and more enjoyable proposition. Today though this film won’t live long in the memory and provides little I can recommend to others, as much as I admire James Stewart.
I can appreciate the performances and the direction, but the lack of resolution left me cold.

Summary: Anatomy of a Murder is a courtroom drama about an attorney who defends a murderer using temporary insanity as a defense. In Michigan, attorney Paul Biegler (James Stewart) is no longer personally invested in his work; instead he focuses on fishing and enjoying time with his alcoholic friend Parnell McCarthy (Arthur O’Connell). However, his attitude changes when he is hired to defend army Lieutenant Frederick Manion (Ben Gazzara) by his wife Laura (Lee Remick). Frederick Manion has recently murdered bar owner Barney Quill with a pistol. While Manion admits that he committed the murder, he initially defends his actions as justified; Quill purportedly raped his wife. However, Biegler points out that unless the murder was committed in self-defense, the murder could not be justified in the court of law. As Manion was not present when his wife was assaulted, and as he committed the murder out of revenge, his actions could not be viewed as self-defense. Therefore, for Manion to be excused for the murder he has to plead insanity as a defense. Opposing Biegler are district attorney Mitch Lodwick (Brooks West) and prosecutor Claude Dancer (George C. Scott). Commentary: Anatomy of a Murder is a stylish drama with fine acting from the entire cast. The use of jazz music by Duke Ellington is perhaps the film’s finest asset. The twists and turns of the plot are clever and keep the drama running smoothly. James Stewart is exuberant as the reinvigorated attorney, Ben Gazzarra is unsavory the pugnacious soldier, Lee Remick is glowing as the flirtatious wife and George C. Scott is imperious as the slick prosecutor. However, the core content of the story is objectionable. The idea that Biegler does not seem to care about whether the person he is defending is innocent or not is already frustrating. Next, the fact that Manion is content with his crime and clearly prone to jealous rage, makes him a deeply unsympathetic character. Further, the fact that the wife is presented as aggressively flirtatious is doubly distasteful. If she was assaulted, the presentation of her behavior is insensitive to assault victims. If she was not assaulted, the woman is obnoxiously manipulative. Then there is Dancer, who appears to be more interested in scoring points for the offense than justice. To the film’s defense, characters in a story do not need to be likable. Nonetheless, the causes that these characters represent are demeaned by the cavalier attitude of the characters. Perhaps, that is the point of the film; the filmmakers could be arguing that the justice system is deeply flawed. However, there are two problems with such an approach. First, bad intentions of the participants in a trial should not serve as accurate indicators of a corrupt system. Second, the narrative of the film is predicated on the idea that the proceedings in the trial are at least interesting, if not very compelling. If the justice system is corrupt and the characters are unpleasant, it is difficult for the viewer to be fully engaged. Still, a film that exposes flaws in the justice system has some utility. In conclusion, Anatomy of a Murder is skillful on its surface and features strong acting; however its content is problematic and its message is muddled.

It's a strange film... ​At first glance, the filmmakers seem to think that the heart of the matter lies in whether the wife of the murderer has been violated or not—except they don't. Justifiably so, as they themselves declare in the movie, since that would still not make the murder permissible. Then they swerve to an after-the-fact plea of temporary insanity on the thinnest of evidence. ​The attorney (Stewart) raises smokescreen after smokescreen regarding the possible rape and the murder victim's character, offering very little to substantiate their central defense claim. This, too, his very character admits. I understand exactly what the film is doing here: it is a deliberate critique of the US legal system and juries, exposing the courtroom as a cynical game where truth takes a backseat to theatrics. ​However, while I get the point, the execution feels far too clinical. Spending nearly three hours meticulously building a courtroom drama only to conclude that the entire system is fundamentally broken—and that the truth doesn't actually matter—almost invalidates the film's own narrative. If the whole process is just an empty sham, watching it play out for that long ultimately becomes uninteresting. Because of this detachment, all the characters remain mere caricatures that we never examine more than skin deep. While the filmmakers likely intended to provoke these exact moral questions, the execution is so dry that it feels like reading a well-argued college essay—intellectually sound, perhaps, but it doesn't make for an engaging film. It's a strange film...

Autopsie d'un meurtre était dans ma watchlist depuis des années. Malgré sa très flatteuse réputation, je trouve que le film ne fonctionne pas, pour différentes raisons : Stewart joue un avocat un peu trop décontracté, fait des blagues sans arrêt au procès, ce qui m'est apparu comme peu vraisemblable. On comprend cependant bien l'objectif de Preminger : montrer que les personnages ne sont pas que des silhouettes là pour incarner une fonction, ils sont des hommes et des femmes qui ont une vie, des passions (la pêche par exemple pour Paul Biegler - Stewart). Le déroulement du procès est conforme à ce qu'on peut attendre de ce type de film -même si j'ai la conviction que la gageure, le défi du métrage est de tenir aussi longtemps sur des échanges de cour, affrontements relativement policés entre les parties. La façon dont est gérée l'affaire centrale -viol ou pas, impulsion irrépressible ou préméditation- manque de matérialité. On ne verra en effet jamais la scène se produire, d'une façon ou d'une autre. Elle est reconstituée dans les dialogues, avec les versions des différents personnages en présence. Cela peut être perçu comme une réussite, pour ma part cela ne donnait pas suffisamment corps à cette affaire. La musique de Duke Ellington -que l'on croise au détour d'une séquence, au piano avec James Stewart-, donne aussi un côté débonnaire à l'histoire. Elle incarne bien le côté surprenant de certains développements -la virée du compère de Stewart au Canada, dont les tenants et aboutissants seront révélés plus tard, ou le personnage de l'accusé joué par Ben Gazzara, qu'on arrive jamais à cerner : joue-t-il la comédie, est-il sincère ? On pourrait penser la même chose du personnage de Lee Remick qui joue sa femme. On peut reconnaître l'accomplissement de Preminger à intéresser le spectateur à un procès qui dure quasiment 2h30 ; mais l'étincelle qui nous fait dire : "là, on est devant quelque chose de grand" ne m'a jamais étreint.

James Stewart is the main reason I watch classics the way I do now. Here he plays a clumsy small town guy who's actually a calculating lawyer, the kind who can coach his client without coaching him and work the jury by pretending to trip over his own words. His performance switches between hesitation, irony and controlled bursts of outrage so naturally that legal jargon ends up sounding like casual conversation. Nothing more unfair than him not taking home Best Actor at the 1960 Oscars. As for the film, it never confirms whether Laura was actually raped or whether the defendant was insane when he pulled the trigger on the alleged rapist. Director Otto Preminger would rather put two equally convincing versions on screen and leave the call to the jury, which is exactly what the law says to do and exactly why the truth doesn't matter. That's the film's biggest strength. Whoever builds the most convincing version inside the rules of the game wins. A matter of "making a lot of noise" versus "racking up all the points," the process of justice or perhaps filmmaking, Otto Preminger's courtroom is a balanced screen and vice versa. The former D.A. (James Stewart) has a fridge full of fish from cooling his heels for a decade, stepping back into the legal arena means less time for jamming with Duke Ellington but also a chance for his colleague (Arthur O'Connell) to crawl out of the bottle. "The lady in the case" (Lee Remick) conceals a shiner behind shades, her husband (Ben Gazzara) is a Korean War vet on trial for shooting her rapist, histories of violence and promiscuity to be pounced on by the prosecutor (George C. Enjoyable and impressively authentic-feeling courtroom drama, though at nearly three hours it did feel a little long. What I liked most was how procedural it is: you really get a sense of how a defense attorney constructs a case rather than simply uncovering “the truth.” The film never cuts away to show us what actually happened, so we are left with the same uncertainty as the lawyers and jury, weighing testimony, credibility and competing versions of events. That ambiguity is one of the film’s real strengths: the point is not that we eventually discover the truth, but that a legal judgment still has to be reached without anyone (except the accuseds) ever being completely sure of it. Some of the social attitudes are fascinatingly dated, particularly the way Lee Remick’s appearance and sexuality become part of the case. There are also some oddly broad comic touches—the dog, in particular—that felt distracting, and I could have done with less of Stewart’s fishing, law-practice troubles and the subplot involving his alcoholic colleague. The Duke Ellington score is fantastic. Jazz seems like an unlikely choice for a courtroom drama, but it gives the film a distinctive energy and is almost worth the watch by itself. A little bloated and occasionally eccentric, but intelligent, entertaining and unusually convincing.

Anatomy of a Murder is a great analysis of the intricacies of case trial from the perspective of the defense. With the defense team being headed by Jimmy Stewart as Attorney Paul Biegler, this film is given a strong character that drives the narrative. Stewart provides another great performance as he shows Biegler as a qualified, intelligent, capable man but one that's a bit eccentric and fronts some levity when necessary. On the prosecutorial team, George Scott plays a good foil to Stewart's Biegler as Assistant Attorney Claude Dancer, equally as intelligent, dogged and determined but a bit less light-hearted. Despite these performances, Anatomy of a Murder is not a character study but a focus on the case at hand, a murder trial. More specifically, we see how the defense builds its own evidence and narratives to sway the jury towards their retelling of events. Despite this angle, Biegler and the defense team are less concerned with proving their client's innocence than they are with proving reasonable doubt and avoiding a conviction. This approach leaves the entire case up to interpretation as no clues are handing over towards innocence or guilt. Overall, this is a great example of a film standing the test of time with a memorable story and approach. Although the performances of Stewart and Scott help the film along, its focus on and approach to its central case layer intrigue upon its plot and force the audience into the positions of attorneys and jurors. Therefore, if you feel like debating a case with the highest fictional stakes, Anatomy of a Murder is the precedent.

This is not the flashiest courtroom drama, which furthers its claim as one of the most accurate cinematic depictions of an American criminal proceeding. In fact, apart from some evidentiary issues (necessary for plot development), it feels remarkably like a Crim law lecture in law school. I love that the screenplay is entirely disinterested in the morals of the proceedings and of the characters involved therein. Instead of setting up a classic "good versus evil" story, it neutrally depicts each character's the flaws and strengths to show their relative impact on the proceeding at issue. This invites the viewer to reflect on the efficacy of our justice system; the question is not whether the defendant committed murder or even whether he should be held to account, but rather whether the the viewer believes that the factors at play (having a charismatic attorney, strategic defamation of witnesses, weighing conflicting expert testimony, etc.) are, in fact, the most germane--or, more cynically, the most practical--considerations for a jury in such a trial.

Anatomy of a Murder forms quite an intriguing investigative drama. This confidently serves up what is perhaps the most comprehensive onscreen treatment of the judicial process. Frank matter-of-fact discussion of the main subject matter must've been quite the shock back in the "squeaky-clean" times of 1959. The counselors don't beat around the bush here. They talk about sex, rape, and murder... for lack of better terms. It's striking how relevant that particular aspect rings nowadays, especially in regard to how lawyers, officers, and judicial figures speak about women in cases involving them in any capacity. While inspired by an actual case circa 1952, the film feels ahead of its time in laying out the information to the audience. Otto Preminger's patient, level-headed direction allows what could've been melodrama to instead become a true-to-life mystery... and a fascinating mental exercise. James Stewart reliably offers yet another excellent performance. It's clever how this film plays with the trusted authority type we'd expect him to fill, notably when the trial gets heated. The ensemble cast acquits themselves superbly (no pun intended). Lee Remmick treads the line between desperate wife and seductive femme like the palm of her hand. Ben Gazzarra spiritedly lends intensity and grit into his defendant, fueling the stakes in his position. George C. Scott, Orson Bean, and Joseph N. Welch steal their scenes with such vivid presence (loud or quiet). The strength of all their performances on top of an astute script already warrants a physical media purchase. Preminger takes it further by developing an absorbing style that enables the back-and-forth to be so engaging. Charm, warmth, intrigue, and crackling dialogue foster strong interest well before the defense accepts their client. The additional layer of ambiguity kept me guessing even while I was fairly certain of how the proceedings would play out. Moreover, any viewer can read each beat, detail, and revelation differently to walk away with varying conclusions, no matter the ultimate ruling. Makes for a haunting ending that leaves a silver lining of sorts. Moody cinematography bathes in the noir aesthetic and adds considerable flair to it. Fantastic framing throughout! Some shots move in the right way at the right time, whether a gradual glide or a frantic snap. Duke Ellington delivers a ritzy jazz score that's also willing to be melancholy at points. Really dug the main menu music on the Criterion DVD, which also rules when heard in its proper context. I would advise against watching this late at night, lest you become sleepy and miss a crucial moment. Its slower burn through 2 hours and 40 minutes does accurately convey how it feels to observe a trial. Your mileage will vary there. One side character's odd detour and a couple repetitive motions stall the momentum a tad. Though I can say overall the film's a far more efficient use of time than actual jury duty. After sorting through and analyzing its intricately stitched pieces, I can attest that Anatomy of a Murder stands as a classic. Viewing several of its genre peers earlier this year (from Philadelphia to Coyote vs. Acme ) may have diluted the impact for me. Nonetheless, it's an excellent picture bearing esteemed influence.

O direito preza por certo formalismo metodológico em torno das normas e pareceres convencionais, buscando certa distância dos aspectos mais humanos do processo. A questão é que, mesmo se utilizando de todos os ornamentos jurídicos (e de outras áreas, gêneros e convenções), o filme não encontra potência no pré-definido. A potência no filme está em como a história é singular à realidade. Nesse pensamento, dá para considerar que Anatomy of a Murder encontra sua potência na performance — que faz parte do direito também, porém com os aspectos mais humanos negados nesse. Dar tempo a cada interpretação e exposição de cada agente do ocorrido central, sem nos revelar o que ocorreu naquela noite, não só nos estimula enquanto espectadores a tentar ver por trás das aparências, mas também possibilita que a realidade experienciada por cada personagem venha à tona. O movimento da câmera segue o movimento do diálogo: enquanto um reestrutura a cena, o outro faz o mesmo com a fala, e daí nasce o ritmo que traz a potência do filme.

From Duke Ellington's sizzling noir soundtrack to James Stewart's magnetically folksy demeanor, Anatomy of a Murder has the components to make a legendary motion picture. Despite the big stars, Otto Preminger, led by Wendell Mayes' rollicking screenplay, gives us something darker, critical, yet exquisitely amoral. Anatomy of a Murder does not attempt to proselytize the virtues or failures of the justice system. Instead it parses out the strategies of a defense, accounts for the varying elements relating to unpredictable human personalities and emotion, presentation of the facts and witnesses, and ultimately leads us to Platonic conclusion of how rhetorical, rather than logical, the American legal system actually is. The movie is not intended to make you feel resolved, and the lingering ambiguities remain as mysterious and subject to conjecture as Laura Manion's heeled shoe found in the trash can. Despite the somewhat dreary outlook, the movie is led by a small-town charismatic lawyer Paul Biegler, played by James Stewart, who uplifts the audience through his character's devotion and cunning. Biegler is a realist, but he's not a pessimist. Sure, he is jaded, having lost his re-election bid for district attorney, and a bit resigned, spending his time fishing and playing piano. But he is far from unmotivated. With a witty tongue and laid-back personality, he seems unshaken through most of the film, openly recognizing the weaknesses and strengths of the facts of the case and accounting for the minute factors that tarnish the supposedly fair legal process. His character, along with his steadfast secretary Maida Rutledge and barely sober but loveable Parnell McCarthy, provide a sense of light in the gray. His client, Frederick "Manny" Manion, is recalcitrant and short-tempered. Accused of murdering Barney Quill for allegedly raping his wife, his blatant jealousy and violent acts in the jail do not help the audience believe Manny was justified. Nor would it convince the jury in the film. Manny's wife Laura Manion does not help the picture: for the standards of that time, she is considered a flirty woman who wears her clothing too tight. Biegler is cognizant of how these issues can affect his case. Biegler counsels Laura to dress modestly, not necessarily because he thinks Laura's fashion has anything to do with the murder, but because he knows how this can come off to a problematic, prejudicial jury. What is most intriguing is that Biegler does not seem to care whether Manny was justified and continues to walk a thin ethical line regarding witness coaching. Biegler inveigles Manny into the irrestible impulse defense, not because it is necessarily true, but because it is the only real legal defense available. However, Biegler's sly witness preparation tactics are fire against the procesecution's fire. For example, Claude Dancer insinuates a false narrative regarding an affair between Quill and Laura, something that even if struck from the record, will not be erased from the jury's mind. The matter of rape becomes a part of deliberations, essential to the defense. But evidence, like torn panties, are hotly scrutinized in cross examinations by Dancer. Biegler's courtroom theatrics and fiery objections are matched by Dancer's intensely hostile methods, resulting in a messy, explosive trial. The movie's climax is a stroke of luck more than it is a recognition of good method. Biegler pulls a hail-mary good-faith witness, (a trope that later became common in these types of exuberant legal dramas). Biegler's only power is persuasion: persuading the judge to overcome the often arbitrary legal obstacles; persuading the witnesses to say and do the right thing; persuading the the easily emotionally manipulated jury prone to the prosecution's smokescreens. The turn at the end demonstrates how many factors can be out of your control at trial when all persuasion has been exhausted. Beigler did all he could. He could only pray thereafter. The movie, although morally gray, ends on a light note. Biegler finds Laura's heel among the rubbish, suggesting her and Manny left in a hurry before they had to pay the lawyer's fees. Manny is concretely imperfect: he's an angry, jealous, violent, dishonest person who ditches his obligations. However, it does not seem fair to have seen him behind bars for Quill's murder. The audience is prone to celebration with the defense. And ironically, Biegler is retained by Pilant to execute Quill's estate, bringing some hope that a private practice has now been established. Despite being ethically questionable as an attorney, Biegler is rewarded. I am not bothered by this. I believe Preminger intended to show, objectively, how imperfect the legal process can be. It is subject to partial authorities, discrimination, and emotional appeal. In many cases, only by pushing the limits of the practice can an attorney triumph against the odds. The boundaries between zealous advocacy and guile are blurred.
